## Introduction ### Overview In Exercises 1--6, you'll continue exploring the RNA-seq results from [this week's lecture](w15a_rnaseq.qmd). In Exercise 7, you'll turn your analysis into a polished Quarto report, practicing with the Quarto material from [week 14](../week14/w14a_quarto.qmd). ::: callout-tip #### Lecture page exercises Make sure to do any of the exercises on this week's lecture page that we did not do in class. Also, if you struggled with any of the exercises we did do in class, go over those again. ::: ### Setting up 1. Open Positron and connect to OSC with your personal dir open ([Setup: starting Positron and connecting to OSC](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#setup-starting-positron-and-connecting-to-osc)). 2. Create a new Quarto document `w15_exercises.qmd` in your `week15` folder, with a YAML header with a title, your name, the date, and `embed-resources: true` ([Creating a Quarto document](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#creating-a-quarto-document)). 3. These exercises build on the DESeq2 object that you saved in the lecture ([Running the DE analysis](w15a_rnaseq.qmd#running-the-de-analysis)). If you didn't run that code yet, do so in your lecture document first. Then, add the following chunk to the top of your exercises document, which will load the packages and recreate the objects from the lecture that you'll need: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DESeq2) library(pheatmap) library(here) library(tidyverse) # Load last (see the lecture) # Load the DESeq2 object that you saved in the lecture dds <- readRDS(here("week15/results/DE/dds.rds")) # Recreate some other objects from the lecture meta <- as.data.frame(colData(dds)) count_mat <- counts(dds) dds_vst <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds) res_rc24 <- results( dds, contrast = c("group", "relictum_24hpi", "control_24hpi") ) res_df <- res_rc24 |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("gene_id") |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> mutate(DEG = padj < 0.05) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## Exercise 1: Gene counts and library sizes 1. How many genes have *mean* counts (across all samples) of at least 10? 2. In the lecture, we computed the "library sizes" (summed gene counts per sample) with `colSums(count_mat)`. That output is not so easy to read or interpret. Instead, get these numbers in millions, rounded to whole numbers, and sorted from low to high. 3. Make a bar plot of the library sizes with _ggplot2_. To plot the counts, you first need a data frame in long format, with one row per gene per sample ([Reshaping data for plotting](../week13/w13b_data-viz.qmd#reshaping-data-for-plotting)). You can create one from `count_mat` as follows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} count_long <- count_mat |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("gene_id") |> pivot_longer( cols = !gene_id, # All columns except 'gene_id' names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count" ) ``` ::: Then, compute the library size of each sample with `group_by()` and `summarize()`, and pipe the result into `ggplot()`. 4. Make a histogram of the `count` column of `count_long`. Why is this plot hard to interpret? 5. Plot `log10(count + 1)` instead. What does the distribution look like now? And why do you think we add 1 to the counts? ## Exercise 2: Volcano plots and outliers In the lecture's volcano plot, one gene stands out with a very high log~2~-fold change. 1. Figure out the identity of this gene by filtering `res_df`. 2. Label this gene in the volcano plot. To do so, add a `geom_text()` layer to the plot from the lecture, with its own `data` argument: a data frame with only this gene. You'll also need to map the `label` aesthetic to the gene ID column. 3. Next, you'll plot the expression levels of individual genes, starting with the most highly significant DEG. First, get the ID of this gene: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_gene <- res_df |> arrange(padj) |> head(n = 1) top_gene$gene_id ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] "LOC120423768" ``` ::: ::: DESeq2 has a plotting function, `plotCounts()`, but its plots are not very good. We will still use that function, but only to quickly extract the counts for our gene of interest in the right format for plotting, using `returnData = TRUE`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_gene_counts <- plotCounts( dds, gene = top_gene$gene_id, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) head(focal_gene_counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output count time treatment S63 1543.81532 24hpi control S64 2279.03704 24hpi cathemerium S65 25.42295 24hpi relictum S66 1105.75009 24hpi control S67 1199.28425 24hpi cathemerium S68 32.14394 24hpi relictum ``` ::: ::: Now, you can make the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_gene_counts |> # Treatment along the x-axis, gene counts along the y, color by treatment: ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) + # Plot separate "facets" with the different time points: facet_wrap(vars(time)) + # Add a boxplot with a partly transparent (alpha) color: geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + # _And_ add individual points: geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) + # Plot styling (e.g., we don't need a legend): theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 4. Make the same plot for the gene with the very high log~2~-fold change. How would you interpret this? 5. Plot one or two more of the most highly significant DEGs. Do they have similar expression patterns across treatments and time points as the top DEG? ## Exercise 3: A customized PCA plot 1. Compare the PCA plot with different numbers of included genes. (Hint: figure out how to do so by looking at the help by running `?plotPCA`.) 2. Customize the PCA plot: can you "separate" treatment and time point (different shapes for one variable, and different colors for the other), like in Fig. 1 of the paper?
{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some hints for PCA plot customization_ In the plot we made in the lecture, each combination of time point and treatment has a distinct color --- it would be better to use **point color** only to distinguish one of the variables, and **point shape** to distinguish the other variable (as was also done in the paper's Fig. 1). To be able to customize the plot properly, we best build it from scratch ourselves, rather than using the `plotPCA` function. But then how do we get the input data in the right shape? A nice trick is that we can use `returnData = TRUE` in the `plotPCA` function, to get plot-ready formatted data instead of an actual plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_df <- plotPCA( dds_vst, ntop = 500, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) ``` ::: With that `pca_df` dataframe in hand, it will be relatively straightforward to customize the plot using your knowledge of ggplot2.
## Exercise 4: More DEGs 1. The paper's Table 1 reports the numbers of **up- and downregulated** DEGs separately. Find these numbers for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison. 2. The paper's Table 1 also reports the number of DEGs with an **absolute LFC \> 1**. Find out how many up- and downregulated DEGs with an absolute LFC \> 1 we have for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison. 3. Extract the results for one or more **other contrasts** in the paper's Table 1, and compare the numbers of DEGs with those in the table. ## Exercise 5: Heatmaps Rather than plotting expression levels for many individual genes, you can create "heatmap" plots to plot dozens (possibly even hundreds) of genes at once. 1. Make a heatmap of the top-25 most highly significant DEGs with the `pheatmap()` function, by running the code below. First, create a vector with the IDs of these genes, by sorting the results table by adjusted p-value, keeping its first 25 rows, and extracting the gene IDs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top25_DE <- res_df |> arrange(padj) |> head(n = 25) |> pull(gene_id) ``` ::: (`pull()` extracts a single column from a data frame as a vector.) Unlike some of the functions in the lecture, `pheatmap()` can't directly use the DESeq2 object: you have to extract and subset the normalized count matrix, and also pass the metadata to the heatmap function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # We need a normalized count matrix, like for the PCA # We can simply extract the matrix from the normalized dds object we created for the PCA norm_mat <- assay(dds_vst) # In the normalized count matrix, select only the genes of interest # ([rows, columns]: select rows by gene ID, and, by leaving it empty, all columns) norm_mat_sel <- norm_mat[top25_DE, ] # Sort the metadata meta_sort <- meta |> arrange(treatment, time) |> select(treatment, time) ``` ::: Now you can create the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pheatmap( norm_mat_sel, annotation_col = meta_sort, # Add the metadata cluster_cols = FALSE, # Don't cluster samples (=columns, cols) show_rownames = FALSE, # Don't show gene names scale = "row", # Perform z-scaling for each gene ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Notes on the code and plot above: - The z-scaling with `scale =` makes sure you can compare genes with very different expression levels: after all, we're interested in relative expression levels across samples/sample groups. - `pheatmap` will by default perform hierarchical clustering both at the sample (`col`) and gene (`row`) level, such that more similar samples and genes will appear closer to each other. Above, we turned clustering off for samples, to keep them in their by-group order. 2. Make a heatmap with the top-25 **most highly expressed** genes (i.e., genes with the highest mean expression levels across all samples).
{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for a hint: how to get that top-25_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} norm_mat <- assay(dds_vst) top25_hi <- names(sort(rowMeans(norm_mat), decreasing = TRUE)[1:25]) ``` :::
## Exercise 6: Adding gene descriptions to the DE results The gene IDs in the results table, like `LOC120423768`, don't tell you much about the genes. The GTF file with the genome annotation, which you explored in [week 4](../week04/w4_exercises.qmd), contains a description for each gene. The following code extracts these into a data frame with one row per gene, and columns `gene_id` and `description`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_descr <- read_tsv( here("garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz"), col_names = FALSE, comment = "#", quote = "", show_col_types = FALSE ) |> filter(X3 == "gene") |> mutate( gene_id = str_extract(X9, 'gene_id "([^"]+)"', group = 1), description = str_extract(X9, 'description "([^"]+)"', group = 1) ) |> select(gene_id, description) ``` ::: 1. Run the code above, and take a look at `gene_descr`. 2. Convert `res_rc24` to a data frame, and move its row names (the gene IDs) into a column called `gene_id` (hint: `rownames_to_column()`). 3. Add the gene descriptions to this data frame with `left_join()` (see [chapter 19 of R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html)), and look at the descriptions of the top-10 DEGs. ## Exercise 7: A polished Quarto report Use the Quarto material from [week 14](../week14/w14a_quarto.qmd) to turn your `w15_exercises.qmd` into a nicely formatted report. 1. Add the following to your YAML header: a table of contents, a theme of your choice, and `execute` options that hide all warnings and messages in the document. 2. Add a header for each exercise, and a sentence or two of Markdown text above or below each plot that describes what it shows. 3. Hide the code (but not the output) of the setup chunk at the top of your document with a chunk option. 4. Give your volcano plot from Exercise 2 a figure caption and a custom width and height ([Figure options](../week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#figure-options)). 5. In your text, report the number of DEGs for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison using **inline code**, so the number is computed when you render the document. 6. Render the document and check that everything looks the way you intended. ## Solutions ### Exercise 1
**1.** Genes with mean counts of at least 10 We need to divide the row sums by the number of samples, which is the number of columns, which we can get with `ncol()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(rowSums(count_mat) / ncol(count_mat) >= 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 12529 ``` ::: ::: Alternatively, you can use the `rowMeans()` function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(rowMeans(count_mat) >= 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 12529 ``` ::: :::
**2.** Library sizes in millions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sort(round(colSums(count_mat) / 1000000)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output S77 S78 S64 S68 S81 S75 S82 S84 S67 S79 S83 S74 S65 S80 S63 S69 S85 S70 S86 S66 9 15 17 18 18 19 19 19 21 21 21 22 23 23 24 24 24 25 25 27 S71 S76 27 29 ``` ::: :::
**3.** A bar plot of the library sizes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} count_long |> group_by(sample_id) |> summarize(lib_size = sum(count) / 1e6) |> # 1e6 = 1 million ggplot(aes(x = sample_id, y = lib_size)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Sample", y = "Library size (millions of counts)") + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
**4.** A histogram of the gene counts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} count_long |> ggplot(aes(x = count)) + geom_histogram() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Nearly all counts end up in the first bar, because most genes have low counts while a few have counts in the millions, which stretches the x-axis.
**5.** A histogram of the log-transformed gene counts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} count_long |> ggplot(aes(x = log10(count + 1))) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: There is a tall peak at 0 (genes with zero counts in a sample), and among the remaining genes, most have between 10 and 10,000 counts. We add 1 because `log10(0)` is `-Inf`, so genes with zero counts couldn't be plotted.
### Exercise 2
**1.** The identity of the log~2~-fold change outlier ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_df |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output gene_id baseMean log2FoldChange lfcSE stat pvalue 1 LOC120431476 39.72038 23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05 padj DEG 1 0.0008584396 TRUE ``` ::: ::: (Interestingly, `res_rc24` contains a second gene with a LFC \> 20, which is not in `res_df` because its `pvalue` and `padj` are `NA`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output baseMean log2FoldChange lfcSE stat pvalue LOC120413430 7.540043 24.46898 5.397990 4.532979 NA LOC120431476 39.720375 23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05 padj LOC120413430 NA LOC120431476 0.0008584396 ``` ::: ::: See the collapsed box "`NA` values in the DESeq2 results table" in the lecture for why p-values can be set to `NA`.)
**2.** Labeling the outlier gene in the volcano plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} outlier <- res_df |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20) res_df |> ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = DEG)) + geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") + # Add the label, in black, and a bit above the point (vjust): geom_text(data = outlier, aes(label = gene_id), color = "black", vjust = -1) + scale_color_manual(values = c("grey60", "firebrick")) + labs(title = "relictum vs. control at 24 hpi") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
Part 3 is a worked example, with the code in the exercise itself.
**4.** Plot the outlier gene ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_gene_counts <- plotCounts( dds, gene = "LOC120431476", intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) focal_gene_counts |> ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) + facet_wrap(vars(time)) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Wow! It looks like in every single time + treatment combination, all but one (or in one case, two) of the samples have zero expression, but there are several extreme outliers. For our focal comparison at `24hpi` (left panel/facet), comparing `control` vs `relictum`, it looks like the difference between these two groups is solely due to the one outlier in `relictum`. Nevertheless, even the multiple-testing corrected p-value (`padj`) is significant for this gene: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> rownames_to_column("gene") |> filter(gene == "LOC120431476") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output gene baseMean log2FoldChange lfcSE stat pvalue 1 LOC120431476 39.72038 23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05 padj 1 0.0008584396 ``` ::: ::: So, we have to be careful with taking our statistical results at face value, and need to visualize important genes!
**5.** Plot more top DEGs For example, for the second most highly significant DEG: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_genes <- res_df |> arrange(padj) |> head(n = 3) plotCounts( dds, gene = top_genes$gene_id[2], intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) |> ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) + facet_wrap(vars(time)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
### Exercise 3
**1.** PCA with different numbers of genes The `ntop` argument sets the number of genes (with the highest variance) to use, which is 500 by default: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 100, intgroup = c("time", "treatment")) plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 5000, intgroup = c("time", "treatment")) ``` :::
**2.** A customized PCA plot First, get the data in the right format, as explained in the hint: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_df <- plotPCA( dds_vst, ntop = 500, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output using ntop=500 top features by variance ``` ::: ::: Second, extract and store the percentage of variance explained by different principal components, so you can later add this information to the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pct_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_df, "percentVar"), 1) pct_var ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 85.3 3.1 ``` ::: ::: Now we can make the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_df |> ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = treatment, shape = time)) + geom_point(size = 5) + labs( x = paste0("PC1 (", pct_var[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", pct_var[2], "%)") ) + scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Infection status") + scale_shape(name = "Time points") + theme_bw() + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
### Exercise 4
**1.** Up- and downregulated DEGs - **Solution using tidyverse/dplyr:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # First we need to convert the results table into a regular data frame as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> # Then we only select the rows/genes that are significant filter(padj < 0.05) |> # If we run count() on a logical test, we get the nrs. that are FALSE v. TRUE dplyr::count(log2FoldChange > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output log2FoldChange > 0 n 1 FALSE 616 2 TRUE 185 ``` ::: ::: - **Solution using base R:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Down-regulated (relictum < control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange < 0 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 616 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Up-regulated (relictum > control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange > 0 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 185 ``` ::: :::
**2.** DEGs with an absolute LFC \> 1 - **Solution using tidyverse/dplyr:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # First we need to convert the results table into a regular data frame as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> # Then we only select the rows/genes that are significant filter(padj < 0.05, abs(log2FoldChange) > 1) |> # If we run count() on a logical test, we get the nrs. that are FALSE v. TRUE dplyr::count(log2FoldChange > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output log2FoldChange > 0 n 1 FALSE 159 2 TRUE 49 ``` ::: ::: - **Solution using base R:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Down-regulated (relictum < control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange < -1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 159 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Up-regulated (relictum > control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange > 1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 49 ``` ::: :::
**3.** Other contrasts For example, for `cathemerium` vs. `control` at 24 hpi: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_cc24 <- results( dds, contrast = c("group", "cathemerium_24hpi", "control_24hpi") ) sum(res_cc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 236 ``` ::: :::
### Exercise 5 Part 1 is a worked example, with the code in the exercise itself.
**2.** A heatmap of the most highly expressed genes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # In the normalized count matrix, select only the genes of interest norm_mat_sel <- norm_mat[top25_hi, ] # Sort the metadata meta_sort <- meta |> arrange(treatment, time) |> select(treatment, time) # Create the heatmap pheatmap( norm_mat_sel, annotation_col = meta_sort, cluster_cols = FALSE, show_rownames = FALSE, scale = "row" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
### Exercise 6
**2.--3.** Adding the gene descriptions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_rc24 |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("gene_id") |> left_join(gene_descr, by = "gene_id") |> arrange(padj) |> select(gene_id, description, log2FoldChange, padj) |> head(n = 10) ``` :::
### Exercise 7
**1--5.** An example of the different elements of the report - The YAML header: ```yaml --- title: "Week 15 exercises" author: "Jane Doe" date: 2026-11-30 format: html: embed-resources: true toc: true theme: cosmo execute: warning: false message: false --- ``` - The setup chunk: ````markdown ```{{r}} #| echo: false library(tidyverse) # [...] ``` ```` - The volcano plot chunk: ````markdown ```{{r}} #| fig-cap: "Volcano plot for relictum vs. control at 24 hpi" #| fig-width: 8 #| fig-height: 6.5 res_df |> ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = DEG)) + # [...] ``` ```` - Inline code to report the number of DEGs: ```markdown We found `r sum(res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` DEGs for the relictum vs. control comparison at 24 hpi. ```
